title: Jubilees: Covenant, Sacred Time, and Restoration - Full Version
subtitle: The Book of Division, kept whole by an African church and read from both sides of the line
description:
Seven years make a week. Seven weeks make a jubilee. And one African church kept the only complete ancient text of the book that counts them.

The Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church calls it Maṣḥafa Kufale, the Book of Division. Most readers know it, if at all, as the "Little Genesis." Jubilees: Covenant, Sacred Time, and Restoration reads it chapter by chapter, with passages from R. H. Charles's translation (made from the Ethiopic) set beside a clear, sourced commentary written for Black readers of the Bible in the United States and for anyone who wants to read alongside them.

It begins with a question many Black readers carry, the "curse of Ham," and reads the story of Noah, Ham and Canaan as Jubilees tells it, including a line that Genesis does not have (7:13). Then it follows the book's own movements: it counts time, it allots the earth, it writes, and it is renewed.

Every reading is marked as a reading. What the text says, what scholars or the Church say, and what the author reads the text to mean are kept apart, so you can always check the page.

What's inside

  • Eight parts, 33 chapters of commentary — from “Which Jubilee?” to “What Jubilees Leaves Us.”
  • The Reading Text — passages from Jubilees in R. H. Charles’s translation (1902; SPCK 1917), printed beside the commentary, with Charles’s own marks kept.
  • Marked pages — the count line, the witness strip that shows which ancient witnesses keep each chapter, “Genesis Beside It” tables, and “Where the English Leaves the Ge’ez.”
  • The Reader’s Charter and “Five Things to Carry” — six lines earned from the chapters, and five things to take out of the book.
  • Hard passages read from both sides of the line — each chapter that reads one tells you so before it begins, and Chapter 31 sets them in one table.
  • An Atlas of the Book, A Timeline, The Foundation Ledger and A Source Guide — with a Glossary, Bibliography and Index.

An honest edition

This is a pre-publication manuscript (v0.9, October 2026). The Reading Text is R. H. Charles’s English translation of Jubilees (1902; SPCK 1917), made from the Ethiopic and in the public domain; it is not a new translation and not an official text of the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church. The book itself says that no reader of Ge’ez has yet checked this English against the manuscripts and that no specialist in Second Temple Judaism has yet read the commentary; its Foundation Ledger records what has and has not been checked. It is an independent work of study and does not speak for any church.

The Reading Text is printed as passages beside the commentary rather than as a continuous edition of all fifty chapters of Jubilees.

Digital edition (PDF), 373 pages. Instant access from your Account page after purchase.
what_you_learn: Which "jubilee" Jubilees means: a measure of time, not the proclamation of liberty in Leviticus 25:10
Why the complete book survives only in Ge'ez, and what the Hebrew, Greek, Latin and Syriac witnesses keep
How Jubilees counts time in weeks, jubilees and a year of 364 days, and why it says the count must not drift
What Jubilees says about Ham and Canaan, including the line at 7:13 that Genesis does not have
How Noah's sons are allotted their lands by lot, and how Canaan's settling reads from both sides of the line
How Jubilees retells Abraham, Jacob and Esau, Dinah and Joseph beside Genesis
How the books of the fathers are handed to Levi to preserve and to renew
What the church that kept the book has said about it, and where the author says it is not known
Five things to carry out of the book, and how to read a hard passage from both sides of the line
who_for:
• Bible readers who have heard of Jubilees, the “Little Genesis,” and want to know what it actually says.
  • Black readers of the Bible who were handed the “curse of Ham” and want to read the story of Noah, Ham and Canaan as Jubilees tells it.
  • Readers of Enoch and the Ethiopian canon who want the next book in the series.
  • Pastors, teachers and small-group leaders who want a sourced reading that marks every reading as a reading.
  • Students and self-learners who like sources, an apparatus and a ledger of what has and has not been checked.

No background in Ge’ez, Hebrew or Greek is needed. Some chapters read hard passages, and each one tells you so before it begins.

faq.question: What format is the book, and how do I get it?
faq.answer: It is a digital PDF edition of 373 pages. After you check out, sign in to your Account page with the email you used to buy and press Download; you can download it again any time.

faq.question: Does it contain the full text of the Book of Jubilees?
faq.answer: It reads the book chapter by chapter and prints passages from Jubilees in R. H. Charles's translation beside the commentary, but it is not a continuous edition of all fifty chapters. It is a study of Jubilees, not a replacement for a complete edition.

faq.question: Is this a finished edition, a new translation, or an official church text?
faq.answer: It is a pre-publication manuscript (v0.9, October 2026). The Reading Text is R. H. Charles's public-domain English translation made from the Ethiopic, not a new translation and not an official text of the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church. The book states that no reader of Ge'ez has yet checked the English against the manuscripts and that no specialist in Second Temple Judaism has yet read the commentary.

faq.question: Do I need to read The Ethiopian Canon or The Book of Enoch first?
faq.answer: No. This volume stands on its own. It is the third book in the same series, and where it touches ground the earlier ones covered, such as the Watchers, the calendar of 364 days or the story of Ham, it says only what the chapter in hand needs and tells you where to read more.

faq.question: Does it deal with difficult passages?
faq.answer: Yes. Jubilees contains hard laws and stories, including a Sabbath law that ends in death, a law that counts a mother's days of uncleanness twice as long when the child is a daughter, the story of Dinah, and passages that tell Israel to keep apart from the nations. The book says plainly what each one does, and each chapter tells you before it begins so that you can stop.

faq.question: Can I read it on my phone or tablet?
faq.answer: Yes. The PDF opens on any phone, tablet, e-reader app or computer, and the book says it is designed to be read on small screens.

faq.question: Can I share my copy or print it?
faq.answer: The Reading Text is a public-domain translation, but the commentary, notes and tables are the author's own work, so please do not copy or redistribute them without permission, apart from brief quotations.
